newsitem.title: USA: Union launches campaign for strawberry workers.
newsitem.headline: Union launches campaign for strawberry workers.

text.p: Seeking to restore its popular appeal of the 1960s, the farm workers union Wednesday kicked off a broad-based campaign to draw attention to the plight of 20,000 California strawberry workers.

The drive to organise the workers, currently the largest in the labour movement, is being backed by 40 groups, including environmental, religious, civil rights and feminist organisations, as well as several celebrities.

"Cesar Chavez created a grand coalition that united behind farm workers in the 1960s," said United Farm Workers of America (UFW) President Arturo Rodriguez. "Today, we kick off a new coalition for the 1990s."
The late Chavez, a UFW founder, brought the problems of farm workers to liberal East Coast households in the 1960s and 1970s by involving them in lettuce and table grape boycotts.
But in the current drive, the UFW and the 78-union AFL-CIO, which is throwing its considerable resources into the effort, are not asking consumers to boycott strawberries.

Instead, the union is hoping to touch off a groundswell of support that will percolate back up the food distribution chain, eventually reaching businesses that deal directly with strawberry growers and handling companies.

"We want them to go their store managers in their local communities," Rodriquez said at an AFL-CIO news conference. "We want them to talk to those store managers and explain to them that strawberry workers deserve the simple, the basic right that we all have and we want in this society."
From the supermarket level, Rodriquez said he hopes that word of consumer sentiment will find its way to the industry.

The workers, whose fields are mostly on California's Central Coast, average $8,500 for a typical April-September season, the UFW said. They are stooped over for 10 to 12 hours a day, exposed to pesticides and housed in substandard facilities with unsanitary bathrooms and drinking water, and many were subjected to sexual harassment, it added.
"Strawberry workers aren't on the bottom step of the economic ladder -- they're not even on the ladder," said AFL-CIO President John Sweeney.

The union, which claims that the strawberry industry has thwarted its workers' desires for union representation, said it would cost consumers only 5 cents more for a pint of strawberries to boost workers' piece pay rates by 50 percent.

The American Farm Bureau Federation accused the UFW of using "misinformation and outright lies" in its depiction of the dire plight of the workers and said the campaign sought to intimidate workers into joining the union against their will.
"Strawberry growers respect the laws on safety and fair treatment of workers in agriculture," California Farm Bureau Federaton President Bob Vice said in a statement.

Although the 26,000-member UFW has won contracts for workers at mushroom, rose, wine grape and vegetable companies, it said strawberry companies have crushed union votes on three occasions by ploughing under the crops and shutting down.
In the next few weeks, the union's campaign is scheduled to appear in several East Coast cities, where much of California's strawberry crop is consumed.
